#3060. Tariffs Pushed Prices Up. Why Retail and Industrial Investors Shouldn't Expect a Quick Reversal

Tariffs are a moving target, and rising costs tend to be sticky, which is bad news for companies and retail customers.

U.S. tariff policy has been unpredictable, which is a big problem for companies and consumers alike. Given the uncertainty, it is difficult for a manufacturer to make long-term plans. That, in turn, is likely to lead to price increases caused by tariffs being sticky. But the truth is, inflation is generally sticky, and companies and consumers shouldn't expect a quick reversal of the impacts of tariffs. Here's what you need to know.

In the third quarter of 2026, industrial giant Caterpillar (CAT -0.84%) reported that tariff costs amounted to $600 million. That was roughly in line with the impact in the third quarter of 2025. At the same time, the company recognized $128 million in tariff recoveries in the third quarter of 2026. There are a lot of moving parts, but the big picture is that tariffs are still a big issue for the heavy equipment manufacturer.

Meanwhile, the company has been facing higher manufacturing costs, driven partly by freight costs. There's a lot that goes into freight costs, notably including today's high energy prices. So there's more going on than just tariffs on the cost front, which is important to consider when you think about the tariff situation reversing.

Notably, consumer staples companies like PepsiCo (PEP +2.23%) have been dealing with input cost inflation, which this snack and soda giant highlighted as an issue in its third-quarter 2026 earnings update. The impact of tariffs and broader inflation is working through the entire supply chain, which is a process that is hard to reverse. Add in the uncertainty around the implementation of tariffs, and companies aren't likely to rush to roll back any price increases they've pushed through.

If you look at tariffs as just another form of inflation, the impact isn't all that difficult to understand. Rising prices flow through the economy, starting with raw materials, moving on to manufacturers, then to retailers, and finally hitting end consumers. At each step along the way, rising costs are passed on to the next entity until they hit your pocketbook.

The costs get passed along because companies are attempting to protect their profit margins. As Cat shows, even with the tariff rebates it collected, it still had to bear significant tariff costs. And, not knowing what to expect next, it makes business sense to continue passing its higher costs on to its customers as best it can. The same is true for PepsiCo or any other company that directly touches consumers. For example, Target (TGT +0.34%) isn't likely to lower prices on products bought overseas if it can't be sure it can maintain that lower price and still make a profit.

Meanwhile, these companies are still facing inflation in other areas. As those costs work through the system, too, protecting margins becomes an even more difficult task. Rolling prices back simply isn't something that companies do quickly, if they do it at all.

Adjusting supply chains isn't a complete solution, either. While that may help companies avoid tariffs, relocating production or sourcing from a different region often entails higher costs. Those costs are baked in and can't be easily reduced, so prices end up permanently higher.

It isn't easy for companies to raise prices. They face pushback throughout the supply chain because nobody wants to pay more for the same thing they bought before. This is why companies like PepsiCo change package sizes while keeping the price the same, which is a way to raise prices without actually announcing a price increase. But once a price increase is implemented and accepted by customers, there is great reluctance to roll it back. Add in the uncertainty around tariffs, and the reluctance to roll back price increases is likely to be even higher. In other words, don't expect a quick reversal of the tariff impact.

#3058. Anthropic Is Expected to List on Nov. 19. I'd Rather Own Amazon Stock Than the IPO.

Why pay up for the Claude maker's shares when the e-commerce giant already collects from it?

Anthropic is expected to start trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT" on Thursday, Nov. 19. Its amended filing on Nov. 10 put the expected price of the 825 million shares between $70 and $78 each.

At the top of the range, the Claude maker could be worth up to around $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis. In May, it announced a funding round at a $965 billion valuation. And Bloomberg said on Nov. 12 that the offering had drawn about six times as many orders as there were shares available.

Amazon (AMZN -0.29%), meanwhile, trades near $267 as I write this, about 7% off its 52-week high. And with the stock at about 25 times its expected 2027 earnings, I think Amazon stock is a better way to get a piece of Anthropic's growth than the initial public offering (IPO) itself.

Amazon will hold over 5% of Anthropic's outstanding shares after the offering, the filing says. But I'd argue the bigger link is the bill Anthropic pays Amazon.

In April, Anthropic agreed to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon between May 2026 and April 2036, no matter how much computing capacity it actually uses. If its spending falls short, it has to pay Amazon the difference.

The commitment covers computing capacity, which Amazon sells through Amazon Web Services (AWS), its cloud computing arm and its biggest source of profit. Showing how much demand AWS is handling, its revenue rose 39% year over year to $46.0 billion in the third quarter, speeding up from 37% in the second quarter. A year before, AWS grew 20%. Even more, AWS operating income climbed 55% to $17.8 billion. It was almost two-thirds of Amazon's total operating income of $28.1 billion.

Amazon's retail and advertising businesses come with that, of course. The company's other two segments, North America and International, made a combined $10.3 billion in operating income in the third quarter.

Advertising took in $19.6 billion in sales for the quarter, up 12% year over year not counting currency changes. That was slower than 22% growth on the same basis a year before, and Amazon said timing around Prime Day hurt the quarter. But Amazon's ad sales in the past four quarters were about $78 billion -- more than double the revenue Anthropic brought in over the same stretch.

All told, Amazon's sales were nearly $800 billion for the last 12 months, and it's worth about $2.9 trillion. So the stock costs around 3.6 times sales.

Of course, the AI build-out isn't cheap. Amazon's free cash flow was negative $42.4 billion in the past 12 months, as its spending on property and equipment jumped. That cash burn may last a while, and it's the biggest risk for the stock.

At the top of its range, Anthropic would be valued at around 40 times its sales in the 12 months through September, which were $35.3 billion. It'd be worth nearly half as much as Amazon, with under a twentieth of Amazon's sales.

Anthropic's growth is still remarkable, but it cooled in the third quarter. Revenue rose 47% from the second quarter, to $17.0 billion. In Q2, it had soared 144%.

Its reported profit fell, too. After an operating profit of $974 million in Q2, Anthropic booked an operating loss of $567 million in Q3. The filing pointed to around $5.0 billion in computing capacity bought on short-term commitments, which costs far more than its multi-year deals, plus $2.0 billion in non-cash charges linked to a donation matching program.

A just-listed stock might also need to absorb lots of fresh supply. Current owners accepted limits on selling (called lock-ups), but they loosen in stages. According to the filing, up to 316 million shares could become eligible for sale right after the offering. And up to 3.3 billion more may become eligible within around six months -- four times the 825 million shares in the IPO.

Ultimately, I don't doubt that Anthropic has quickly built an impressive business. But at up to around 40 times sales, the IPO price relies on that growth staying fast for a long time.

Amazon, though, already gets a piece of Anthropic's growth from its stake and the AWS contract, plus retail and ad businesses that earned $10.3 billion in the third quarter alone. At around 25 times next year's expected earnings, I'd rather own Amazon stock than buy into the IPO.

#3056. Is Nvidia Worth This Much Less Without Jensen Huang?

Nvidia stock dropped nearly 13% this week.

Last Sunday, Nvidia (NVDA -2.01%) co-founder and then-CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair with someone who is an alleged Chinese spy. In the following days, The New York Times reported that Huang also had an affair with a direct report. On Thursday, Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation.

At its peak, Nvidia had a market cap of $5.8 trillion. At market close on Friday, the stock had a market cap of $3.93 trillion. The stock is down 13% over the past week and 6% since Wednesday’s market close.

So, investors think Nvidia is worth less without Huang in the corner office. Are they right?

There's no doubting the impact that Jensen Huang had on Nvidia's technical abilities. He steered the company to develop cutting-edge products in the GPU realm, along with other products to support them. Nvidia's technology is best-in-class, and with Huang stepping down from the CEO role, that fact likely won't change.

Furthermore, while Huang is unique, there are likely a handful of people within the Nvidia organization that could take over and do a great job.

The best company at leadership transitions has been Apple (AAPL +0.39%), as it has gone through several transitions and sustained its dominance every time. While Nvidia's situation may be a bit more tumultuous than anything Apple has dealt with, Nvidia can survive.

So, investors need to make a decision about Nvidia stock. Is the only reason you invested in it because of Jensen Huang? Or is it because of Nvidia's leading technology and position within the massive AI build-out?

For me, I invested in Nvidia because of its products and positioning, although having Huang at the helm was a nice touch. The core of my Nvidia investment thesis is still intact, and even though my position is dipping due to the news breaking this week and investors panic-selling, I'm still holding course because the business will likely be just fine.

During last quarter's conference call, Nvidia gave guidance for 70% revenue growth in 2027. Normally, companies don't issue guidance six months in advance, but it's likely that Nvidia has pretty much all of the orders it expects to receive locked in for 2027. It's extremely unlikely that companies will start to cancel orders because of Huang's actions or resignation, so investors should be able to count on that projection.

Furthermore, the product development pipeline is already set for many years in advance. So, what's coming out is already influenced by Huang's fantastic technical mind.

Even though losing Jensen Huang will hurt Nvidia, I think the business is still a great one and in a fantastic position to deliver incredible returns going forward. Just look at how cheap Nvidia's stock has gotten due to the sell-off.

NVDA PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

Nvidia trades at about 10 times next year's earnings estimates, which is an incredibly cheap price tag for any stock, let alone one of the world's most dominant companies.

While it may take a few months for the storm surrounding Huang to subside, the market will eventually get back to valuing Nvidia's business for what it is, and the stock could provide major upside as a result. I'm not selling my Nvidia shares right now, and I don't think most investors should, either.

#3054. Prediction: Archer Aviation Will Fly Paying Passengers Before the 2028 Olympics. Here’s What $5,000 Invested Today Could Be Worth by Then.

Archer is on its way to putting paying passengers in the air before the Games.

Los Angeles is widely considered to be one of the most traffic-congested cities in America. Hollywood has made a running joke of it for decades (La La Land, anyone?), and goodness knows -- certainly the Angelenos know it -- how many hours have been blown in stop-and-go traffic, whether rush hour or not.

If we can all agree that the traffic in L.A. is bad, then we can pretty much imagine the gridlock awaiting the city's freeways when the Summer Olympics arrive in July 2028.

If, indeed, traffic is not bad, then Archer Aviation (ACHR -6.93%) may be one reason for it. And if my prediction comes true -- and Archer carries paying passengers above L.A. before the Olympic flame is lit -- investors who put $5,000 into this industrial stock today could have plenty of reasons to celebrate.

Archer Aviation is one of the frontrunners in the nascent eVTOL market. "eVTOL" stands for electric vertical takeoff and landing, and Archer's aircraft do exactly that: They lift up vertically like helicopters, then transition into forward flight in the manner of an airplane. That sentence can hardly convey the engineering complexity involved in making such a transition, much less doing it safely with four paying passengers and a pilot on board.

Archer hasn't, to be sure, demonstrated that its eVTOL (Midnight) can transition from vertical to forward flight with a pilot in the front seat, though it does expect to do so before the end of the year. It goes without saying, then, that Archer also doesn't have the regulatory green light to fly paying passengers, one reason why it reported a net loss of about $275 million in the third quarter.

There are, however, reasons to believe Archer will have solved these challenges before the 2028 Olympics, when the company is expected to serve as the official air taxi provider.

First off, Archer is already in the fourth and final stage of the FAA's type certification process, arguably the most important regulatory milestone yet. If it can acquire this certification, Archer will be authorized to operate Midnight commercially, provided it also obtains subsequent operational approvals. The fourth stage is admittedly pretty extensive -- it involves a lot of testing -- but with nearly two years before the Olympics, Archer has time to secure these approvals before the torch is lit.

Archer may, in fact, be able to carry passengers before it finishes the fourth stage, thanks to the federal government's eVTOL Integration Pilot Program (eIPP). The program, which also includes Archer's rivals Joby Aviation and Beta Technologies as participants, allows Archer to work directly with the FAA to introduce limited passenger operations before it completes the standard certification process. Indeed, Archer recently received a special airworthiness certificate allowing it to pilot demonstration flights in Los Angeles, which the company expects to start in 2026.

Finally, Archer has already begun building infrastructure in Los Angeles in preparation for its role as the official air taxi provider. This has included securing control of Hawthorne Municipal Airport and planning takeoff and landing sites across the city.

So, what will Archer stock, currently trading at sub-$5 a share, be worth by the 2028 Summer Olympics?

My prediction: I think Archer will at least double to $10 a share if it has commercial flights underway by the Olympics. That would put its market cap (currently about $4 billion) near $9 billion, accounting for the roughly 155 million additional shares expected to be issued in its pending acquisition of Boeing's aviation subsidiaries. For perspective, Joby Aviation is currently valued at $6 billion, and it also doesn't have a certified commercial eVTOL in service.

Thus, if someone were to invest $5,000 today, doubling would put that investment at about $10,000 by July 2028.

Of course, this is an estimate based on today's situation, which can change. Archer still faces a mountain of challenges, not the least of which is manufacturing eVTOLs and navigating cash burn. Still, if Archer can turn its ambitious plans into an operating air taxi service, investors who get on board today could be rewarded handsomely.

#3053. Ray Dalio says Bessent move is sign that a debt crisis is getting closer; recommends gold and bitcoin

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's debt buyback announcement this week fits into a broader pattern that can signal a forthcoming crisis, according to billionaire investor Ray Dalio.

The Bridgewater Associates founder said Bessent's plan to increase government debt purchases may portend trouble for the U.S. economy. Coupled with the Japanese government reducing its U.S. bond market exposure and surging long-dated American bond yields, Dalio said investors may want to prepare their portfolios for increased risk by owning cryptocurrencies and gold.

"I am confident that the government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote in a LinkedIn post published Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Dalio noted that the Treasury Department has "only limited capacity" to buy back bonds. Bessent told CNBC on Thursday that his team was going to "make a market" and that the purchases would likely top $4 billion.

The U.S. is spending about 40% more than it's bringing in, resulting in the burgeoning budget deficit, Dalio said. The U.S. budget deficit topped $432 billion in July, but Bessent told CNBC that it's likely peaked under President Donald Trump's administration.

Bessent said in the interview that a team was looking at ways to shrink spending by hundreds of billions of dollars. But Dalio said there is "very little ability" to do so given that it is either committed or considered essential.

After years of overspending, Dalio said total debt now dwarfs what the U.S. brings in each year. If the U.S. government was a business, Dalio said debt service payments would come in at roughly $11 trillion — about 200% of annual revenue.

Dalio, 77, warned the cost of repaying principal and servicing the debt will only grow over time.

To solve this, Dalio said the U.S. needs to carefully employ a three-part strategy to get the budget deficit down to 3% of gross domestic product.

First, Dalio said the U.S. government needs to reduce its spending. Second, he said tax revenue needs to be raised. Finally, the New York native and Harvard Business School alumni said lower interest rates were needed.

"All three need to happen concurrently so as to prevent any one from being too large," Dalio said. "If any one is too large, the adjustment will be traumatic."

Dalio cautioned against ramming through these adjustments by "force." For instance, "it would be very bad if the Federal Reserve unnaturally forced interest rates down," he said.

Dalio said it's important to to take steps now, while the economy is healthy. An economy in recession requires increased government spending, he said.

Dalio said the exact timing of a debt crisis can be swayed by variables ranging from military conflict to political change. On its current trajectory, the U.S. could enter such a crisis in as early as one year or as late as five. "My guess, which I suppose will be a bad one, is that it will come in three years, give or take two, if the course we're on is not changed."

To prepare, Dalio recommended investors are underweight debt assets, such as bonds.

As much as 10% to 15% of a portfolio could land in gold, as well as "a bit" of bitcoin, the hedge fund founder said.

Dalio's post came at the tail end of a volatile week for U.S. financial markets. Rising long-term Treasury yields have pressured stocks, leading the S&P 500 to snap a a three-week-long advance.

#3052. Anthropic’s S-1 Says Natural Gas, Not Chips, Is AI’s Biggest Bottleneck. Here’s the Stock That Sells the Engines.

Natural gas companies don't need a particular AI model to win out; they'll win if demand for natural gas from data centers continues to rise.

Anthropic's S-1 filing revealed that power is still one of the biggest bottlenecks for artificial intelligence (AI) companies. For investors, that makes natural gas stocks particularly attractive, as Anthropic mentioned natural gas five times in just one paragraph in its filing.

There are a few ways to capitalize on that opportunity, ranging from owning shares of natural gas producers to owning shares of companies that own and operate pipelines and supply gas to data center campuses. One I'd lean toward is Energy Transfer (ET -0.10%), which operates over 140,000 miles of pipelines and associated energy infrastructure across 44 states.

There's no publicly available information that Energy Transfer is connected to Anthropic. Rather, the bigger takeaway about natural gas from Anthropic's S-1 filing is how a company like Energy Transfer can benefit.

Anthropic even notes that being unable to secure gas supply and transportation during facility development could cause "a planned site to be delayed or abandoned." That's a huge risk: not only to have a site delay when trying to create advanced AI models, but to potentially have to abandon a site completely. And that risk shows why access to natural gas is so important.

Anthropic and its rival, OpenAI, which may go public in 2027, will win by having the best AI models. But Energy Transfer only needs AI use cases and adoption to increase to win, as it will create more power demand from AI companies. While the AI story is still in its early stages, it looks as if that's happening. According to research from The Motley Fool, 26.8% of U.S. businesses used AI in October 2026, compared with 3.7% in September 2023.

Energy Transfer is already capitalizing on that demand by signing an agreement with Oracle to supply natural gas to three of its data centers in the United States. It also has an agreement to provide a Nexus Data Center hyperscale campus with natural gas, as well as a 20-year binding agreement with Entergy Louisiana, a subsidiary of Entergy, to provide natural gas to its facilities in Louisiana. In a roundabout way, that connects Energy Transfer to Meta Platforms, as Meta is partnering with Entergy Louisiana to power a data center facility.

One of the biggest risks associated with Energy Transfer's AI opportunities is that building out pipelines and infrastructure could yield lower-than-expected returns.

Long-term debt is at $68.8 billion, a byproduct of building and expanding its extensive energy pipeline network. The debt is manageable as long as profits continue to grow, as we saw in the third quarter of 2026. For the third quarter, Energy Transfer's adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) grew 31% from the prior-year period to $5 billion, which suggests the company's investments are paying off. But if debt keeps climbing while EBITDA falls, it's reasonable to question if the spending is justified.

With that understanding, there's still a lot to like about the company, including its 7% dividend yield and a dividend payout that has increased for 20 consecutive quarters. And as for where the stock price could head next, analysts are generally bullish. According to CNN-tracked data, of the 26 analysts who cover the stock, the median one-year price target is $25, representing a 28.6% gain from the Nov. 10 closing price of $19.43.

#3051. Is Cisco Systems a Buy After Its Latest Earnings Report?

For many investors, the company's beat-and-raise first quarter wasn't as impressive as it looked.

After market close Thursday, Cisco Systems (CSCO -6.24%) delivered a beat-and-raise quarter, posting double-digit percentage gains in key fundamentals. It also notched new records in certain line items. So, given all that winning, the stock logically traded higher the following day, right?

Wrong. Investors, accustomed to robust growth and estimates-beating quarters from tech hardware companies, found several developments in the earnings report concerning. Meanwhile, events outside of the company's control were putting the hurt on industry stocks on Friday, and Cisco's shares fell by more than 6%. That's quite the dichotomy, so here's a look at where that places the stock just now.

In Cisco's first quarter of fiscal 2027, it earned $18.5 billion in revenue, setting a new all-time high. That figure was also up 24% year over year. Net income not under generally accepted accounting principles (non-GAAP, or adjusted) saw an even bigger leap, improving by 39% to $5.6 billion ($1.40 per share).

Both figures topped consensus analyst estimates, though not overwhelmingly. On average, Cisco-tracking pundits were modeling revenue of slightly over $18.1 billion, and adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $1.32.

One of the primary drivers of the company's revenue growth was, unsurprisingly, the build-out of artificial intelligence (AI) compute capacity. On the bottom line, profitability was helped by a workforce reduced by layoffs.

In its earnings release, the company quoted CEO Chuck Robbins as saying that "Organizations are turning to Cisco for our trusted, market-defining technology and our expertise to help them scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era."

"We are in the very early stages of a multi-year networking supercycle, and we're confident in our ability to continue capturing the multi-billion-dollar opportunity it represents for Cisco," he added.

That confident talk was backed by a guidance raise. Cisco management now expects full-year fiscal 2027 revenue of $74.8 billion to $75.8 billion; its previous forecast was $72.2 billion to $73.4 billion. The adjusted EPS estimate also received an upgrade, to a range of $5.47 to $5.53 (up from $5.05 to $5.11).

Amid these positive developments, savvy investors identified several trends they didn't find to be so sunny. Total product orders, which matter for a hardware purveyor like Cisco, rose 21% year over year in the first quarter. That's solid, but it was well under the 35% in the fourth quarter of 2026. This was understandable, as hyperscaler clients were over-busy in the company's fourth quarter; their orders during the period soared to $4 billion. Regardless, a notably declining growth rate is exactly what shareholders don't want to see with a hardware maker.

Additionally, adjusted gross margin fell far enough to notice. Due to higher costs for memory components and a greater contribution from lower-margin AI networking products to overall revenue, it dipped to 65.6% from the year-ago figure of 68.1%.

Trailing performance matters less than future performance, of course, but some coming quarters might be a bit cloudy for Cisco. On the conference call discussing the first-quarter results, CFO Mark Patterson noted the anticipated "tougher compares and a little bit less visibility" the company expects in the second half of the new fiscal year.

Another short-term negative factor isn't the company's fault. That's the sudden emergence and fallout of the Jensen Huang scandal. Huang, a co-founder and the longtime CEO of bellwether AI chipmaker Nvidia (NVDA -2.01%), became embroiled in a situation involving an alleged spy from China, and stepped down from his post. While Cisco and Nvidia compete in certain product segments, they are also business partners in several hardware segments. Anytime a company's leader exits the scene, questions immediately arise about the continuity of the business' strategy. So far, there's been no indication that interim CEO Colette Kress will shake up Nvidia's existing plans. Still, she hasn't promised allegiance to Huang's goals and desires for the company, either.

I think the reaction to the negative aspects of the earnings release overshadowed its many positives -- not least those deep-in-the-double-digits growth rates, and the usual high-margin net income figure. That guidance raise was nothing to sneeze at either, and I'd be encouraged by management's conviction that the encouraging growth rates should continue. We should also bear firmly in mind that spending on AI build-outs can be lumpy, given the continuing frenzy of this arms race and the urgency of advancing such projects. I'm not concerned about the ups and downs in order growth, and folks considering a Cisco buy shouldn't be either. This moment feels like a good opportunity to get a long-time and trusted hardware supplier at a discount.

I was one of the first to see JetBlue’s new domestic first class cabin. Here’s what it was like on board.

Editor/Content Strategist & Smart Travel Podcast Host

JetBlue Airways’ long-awaited domestic first class seats will take to the skies in December 2026, but I got a peek at the new BlueFirst cabin before it launched. There was plenty to love, but there were some downsides as well.

The addition of domestic first class is a major change for the airline, which has introduced a slate of new premium products in recent years like its BlueHouse airport lounges. The entirety of JetBlue’s fleet — except for planes that already have lie-flat Mint business class seats installed — is getting the new domestic BlueFirst recliner seats up front. Up until now, they’ve only had standard and extra-legroom economy seats.

For JetBlue flyers, the new seats will offer an elevated experience that has been missing on most domestic flights. The wider seats are more comfortable and have more legroom than any seat in economy. BlueFirst passengers will also get premium amenities and cold food options.

While I didn’t fly on the plane, JetBlue invited me to tour its first aircraft with the new seats — an Airbus A320 known as “Blue Kid in Town” — before it starts flying Dec. 8, 2026. Here’s what it was like onboard.

JetBlue’s BlueFirst cabin on the A320 has 12 seats — three rows in a two-by-two configuration. That means each passenger will either be in an aisle or a window seat. (Its non-Mint A321 planes will have an extra row of BlueFirst for a total of 16 seats.)

Compared to the economy cabin, the first class seats are wider, have more legroom and come with extra recline. They also have a three-way adjustable headrest.

On all flights with BlueFirst, JetBlue crew members will bring a box of amenities around for passengers to choose from. Options include crew socks, earbuds, mouthwash packets and OSEA skincare products, including lip balm, hand cream and pulse point oil.

Domestic first class typically doesn’t offer additional amenities, so this is a nice touch.

JetBlue said in its Q3 2026 earnings call that the majority of its planes will have BlueFirst installed by the end of 2027, although the rollout won’t be completed until 2028.

You can book BlueFirst by purchasing a ticket or by redeeming points and miles, including with JetBlue’s own TrueBlue points. Mosaic elite members and JetBlue Premier Card holders traveling on eligible fares can get complimentary BlueFirst upgrades if there are seats available at 60 minutes before departure.

» Learn more: Your guide to flying JetBlue BlueFirst

As a frequent flyer, I strongly believe the most important thing about a premium product is seat comfort. Even if an airline offered the best catering in the sky, an uncomfortable seat is a deal breaker.

Thankfully, JetBlue nailed it with its new BlueFirst seats. The seats are extremely cozy and have a tufted design, which makes it feel like you’re sitting on a couch. That feeling is enhanced by the light-gray synthetic leather used for the seat, which mimics the look of fabric.

The airline incorporated “flex foam” from the mattress company Tuft & Needle into the seat, which contours to the customer’s body shape but bounces back after use. (JetBlue worked with Tuft & Needle on its Mint seats as well.) I found the seats to be extremely comfortable.

There were also multiple storage options at the seat, which I appreciated, including under the seatback screen and beneath the armrest. Older first-class seats often don't have much storage, but airlines have rectified that in their newer products.

I also loved the playful terrazzo-style material JetBlue used for the armrest table. There’s also a drinks tray that pops out from the center console, which uses the same material.

JetBlue says the absence of a divider is because it is an egalitarian airline, but the lack of separation between the two cabins makes it feel like less of an upgrade. It also means BlueFirst passengers will have to deal with passengers from economy coming up to the front to speak with flight attendants or use the lavatory.

BlueFirst features 13.3-inch seatback screens that are equipped with Bluetooth connectivity. There are also USB-A and USB-C ports under the seatback screen, in addition to a standard electrical outlet.

JetBlue is also debuting a creative use of the seatback screen called Mixologist Mode, which allows you to customize your own cocktail. If you just want a simple beverage, you can also order it via the screen, instead of using the call button.

To make room for BlueFirst, JetBlue had to make changes to its economy cabin, including a reduction of pitch (the distance between seats on a plane).

JetBlue has long been recognized as the U.S. airline offering the most legroom for standard economy passengers, which is expected to change with the addition of BlueFirst.

It’s also removing two rows of EvenMore seats, which feature extra legroom and premium perks in economy. Mosaic elites can select these seats at booking or at check-in, depending on their status level, so that means less chances of scoring an EvenMore seat as an elite.

At the preview, JetBlue showcased its food and beverage options for BlueFirst, from upgraded snacks to its bento-inspired meal options.

I didn’t feel strongly about any of the snack options, although the Sockerbit Swedish sour gummy candies were a big hit. However, the meal boxes, which JetBlue is calling FirstFare, were delicious.

Passengers will have two different breakfast or dinner options, depending on what time and which direction you’re flying. My favorite box was the dinner on eastbound and northbound flights, offering sesame beef noodles with crispy wontons, a Szechuan dip and macarons.

For breakfast on those flights, one option is a sweet potato and bean breakfast bowl with guacamole and hot sauce, alongside poached pear and a blueberry chia pudding.

Many attendees agreed the highlight of the desserts was the carrot caramel cake offered on westbound and southbound flights for dinner.

If you have dietary restrictions, JetBlue will also offer kosher options, as well as vegan and gluten-free ones.

JetBlue got some criticism when it announced that it wouldn’t offer hot meals for BlueFirst customers. Full-service carriers typically offer warmed nuts before a hot entree alongside a salad and dessert for the meal.

However, this didn’t bother me at all. I often find airline meals extremely heavy, especially when you’re essentially just sitting in a chair for several hours without doing anything. The cold meal options were light and refreshing, which I appreciated.

While I didn’t experience the food on a real flight, I would imagine serving cold dishes eliminates the awful smell that permeates the cabin whenever flight attendants begin warming up the meals. If so, it’s a win in my book.

Ultimately, BlueFirst is worth it for people who want that extra space at their seat, from more legroom to greater recline. However, I probably wouldn’t splurge for BlueFirst on shorter routes that don’t come with a meal.

JetBlue now offers base, standard and flex fares, including for BlueFirst tickets. If you select the cheapest base option, you will get only one free checked bag, and you'll need to pay a fee for any changes and cancellations. You'll also earn fewer TrueBlue points per $1 spent, and you won't be able to select a seat for free until 24 hours before departure.

#3049. Planning to Claim Social Security at 62? Here Are 3 Critical Questions to Ask Yourself First

Before taking benefits as early as possible, make sure you know what you're getting into.

When you sit down to plan for retirement, one of the things you'll need to do is figure out when to claim Social Security. And the good news is that you have plenty of options.

Once you turn 62, you can claim benefits at any time. If you want to ensure that those benefits are not reduced, you'll have to wait until full retirement age to file, which is 67 if you were born in 1960 or later.

You can also delay your Social Security claim past full retirement age for boosted benefits. Each year you hold off until your 70th birthday gives your benefits a guaranteed 8% increase for life.

Claiming Social Security at 62 can be tempting because it means getting your money as early as possible. But it also means accepting smaller checks. So before you move forward with a claim at 62, make sure to address these important questions.

You might assume that once you retire, your annual income needs will drop substantially. But once you sit down to create a budget, you may realize that's not actually the case.

While certain costs of yours may drop in retirement due to not having to go to an office on a regular basis, many of your core expenses are likely to stay the same. Some, like healthcare and entertainment, might even increase.

It's important to get a solid handle on your estimated spending to see whether you can afford to take a hit on your Social Security benefits by filing early. And don't forget to account for one-off expenses, like home repairs that might arise out of the blue or annual car insurance payments. A detailed budget could help you arrive at the right choice.

Ideally, Social Security won't be your only available source of income in retirement. Once you've identified your annual spending needs, see how much income you can expect outside of those benefits.

Let's say you expect to safely withdraw $30,000 a year from your retirement savings and anticipate another $5,000 a year in interest income. If your annual spending needs are $60,000, you'll need $25,000 from Social Security. If filing for benefits at 62 won't leave you with $25,000 annually, you'll know that signing up then is a mistake -- especially if waiting until full retirement age lets you easily meet your income goals.

It's not necessarily so difficult to sit down and create a retirement budget. It's also not that hard to estimate your annual non-Social Security income.

Figuring out how long you expect to live is a lot trickier. In fact, it's downright impossible. But you can use your health and family history to make an educated guess.

Here's why that's important. If you believe you're likely to live a longer life, claiming Social Security at 62 may not just reduce your benefits on a monthly basis. It could also leave you with less Social Security over your lifetime.

On the flip side, if you're not sure whether filing at 62 is the right choice but have health problems and don't expect to live a long life, you may end up with more Social Security in total if you take benefits early rather than wait. So it's definitely crucial to factor in your health and your parents' lifespans.

Some people might tell you that claiming Social Security at 62 is a dangerous move. The reality is that it could be, but that's not a given. The key is to figure out how an early claim might impact your ability to cover your costs, and whether it's likely to lead to a smaller lifetime benefit. Only once you've addressed these factors can you make an informed decision.

#3046. Dejounte Murray requests trade from Pelicans

After two-plus seasons, Dejounte Murray's time in New Orleans may be coming to a close.

ESPN's Shams Charania reported Friday that the veteran point guard has requested a trade, with the Pelicans confirming the news shortly thereafter. This comes on the heels of two blowout defeats for the Pelicans: a 51-point thrashing by the Warriors on Monday, followed by a 34-point loss to the Nets on Wednesday.

In their statement, the Pelicans said that they will "evaluate potential trade opportunities that are in the best interest of our organization."

Murray has appeared in nine games this season, averaging 13.4 points, 4.6 rebounds, 4.4 assists and 1.6 steals in 31.4 minutes per game. He's started alongside second-year guard Jeremiah Fears, whom many view as the Pelicans' point guard of the future.

Murray missed three games in late October/early November for personal reasons, and the Pelicans won all three, with Fears flourishing and Herb Jones providing quality defensive play as the replacement in the starting lineup. In a since-deleted social media post, Murray responded to a post noting the Pelicans' record in the games he missed, saying, "From what's going on INSIDE, this sounds like someone hit you to say this! THE 'SABOTAGE' IS REAL!"

Acquired from the Hawks during the 2024 offseason, Murray has appeared in 54 games for the Pelicans over two-plus seasons. His 2024-25 campaign was cut short by an Achilles tendon rupture, which also sidelined him for most of the 2025-26 season. He had already been ruled out for Friday's game against the Grizzlies with an ankle injury by the time reports of a trade request surfaced.
